item.description: Jim Simons · Slaves to the model — Discipline handed to the system. The best-returning fund on record forbids its brilliant people from improvising. This piece asks who that rule is actually protecting against.

item.title: Jim Simons · Beauty, and the best people
item.description: Jim Simons · Beauty, and the best people — He published his own principles. A man who made his fortune out of algorithms summed up a career in five principles. Not one of them is about mathematics.

item.title: Socrates · Not supposing that you know
item.description: Socrates · Not supposing that you know — The whole margin is that thin. The poster says he knew that he knew nothing. This page is about the narrower and far more useful thing he said.

item.title: Socrates · The midwife's trade
item.description: Socrates · The midwife's trade — No answers, only delivery. His mother delivered babies and he said he had inherited the trade. This page is about why he withheld answers.

item.title: George Soros · Reflexivity
item.description: George Soros · Reflexivity — Perception rewrites the thing. Textbooks say prices reflect fundamentals. This piece asks why Soros says the arrow runs both ways, and how that loop manufactures a bubble.

item.title: George Soros · Knowing when you're wrong
item.description: George Soros · Knowing when you're wrong — Not right or wrong, but how much. A man famous for enormous bets credits his survival to admitting mistakes. This piece asks why those two things are not in conflict.

item.title: The Sovereign Individual · The logic of violence
item.description: The Sovereign Individual · The logic of violence — Institutions follow costs. This book explains a thousand years of institutions without ideas and without great men. One variable does the whole job.

item.title: The Sovereign Individual · From citizen to customer
item.description: The Sovereign Individual · From citizen to customer — Jurisdictions start competing. Written in 1997, the book predicts governments will have to compete. This is the chain that gets them there, and who pays.

item.title: Strategies of the Warring States · Burning the bonds
item.description: Strategies of the Warring States · Burning the bonds — Buying what the ledger cannot hold. The man sent to collect the debts burned the contracts instead. This is about how that apparently pure loss was finally settled.

item.title: Strategies of the Warring States · Zou Ji at the mirror
item.description: Strategies of the Warring States · Zou Ji at the mirror — Three people praise you, three motives. Wife, concubine and guest all said he was the handsomer man. This is about the three different things he heard in one answer.

item.title: Su Shi · No wind, no rain, no sun
item.description: Su Shi · No wind, no rain, no sun — Switching off the scoring. Everyone else on the road was miserable. He was not. What exactly did he switch off in that moment?

item.title: Su Shi · Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou
item.description: Su Shi · Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou — Doing real work where you were sent to rot. Asked at the end of his life to name what he'd accomplished, he named three places he'd been banished to. Why those?

item.title: Su Shi · I see no bad people
item.description: Su Shi · I see no bad people — Treating a person as a person. A man whose enemies nearly had him executed said he could see no bad people anywhere. This is not naivety.

item.title: Su Shi · Clear the ground first
item.description: Su Shi · Clear the ground first — The first thing he did when the salary stopped. Exiled to Huangzhou, his salary essentially gone. The first thing he did was not write poetry.

item.title: Su Shi · The mud had to go somewhere
item.description: Su Shi · The mud had to go somewhere — Turning the by-product into the thing. Dredging a lake leaves you holding the mud. What he did with it is still there a thousand years later.

item.title: Su Shi · I dare not write
item.description: Su Shi · I dare not write — Stopping the defence is a decision. After his own words were used to build a case against him, did he keep writing? The question is which kind he stopped.

item.title: Su Yu · Daring to say it plainly
item.description: Su Yu · Daring to say it plainly — How to overturn an order from above. The strategy settled above him sent his force south across the river. This is how a subordinate turned a standing order around.

item.title: Su Yu · Turning a small plan into a large one
item.description: Su Yu · Turning a small plan into a large one — Enlarging when the opening appears. The name of the campaign came from his telegram. This is about how an operation got enlarged into a decisive battle while it was running.

item.title: Sun Tzu · Win first, then fight
item.description: Sun Tzu · Win first, then fight — The work happens before the clash. Everyone quotes it as bravado. Read slowly it says the opposite: by the time you are fighting, it is mostly decided.

item.title: Sun Tzu · Know both, and know which is harder
item.description: Sun Tzu · Know both, and know which is harder — Your own numbers are the flattered ones. Quoted for two thousand years, usually as a case for research. The half everybody skips is the one about yourself.

item.title: Sun Tzu · The best fight is the one nobody has
item.description: Sun Tzu · The best fight is the one nobody has — Winning a hundred times is not the top of the list. A hundred victories sounds like the ceiling. He says it isn't, and the reason is arithmetic rather than modesty.

item.title: Sun Tzu · The flank only works if the front holds
item.description: Sun Tzu · The flank only works if the front holds — A clever move on its own is a donation. Everyone wants the unexpected move. The chapter is mostly about the unglamorous thing it has to stand on.

item.title: Sun Tzu · Take the shape of what you meet
item.description: Sun Tzu · Take the shape of what you meet — Avoiding the strong part is the hard half. 'Be like water' became a poster. The chapter is stricter than the poster, and most of it is about what not to do.

item.title: Nassim Taleb · The turkey problem
item.description: Nassim Taleb · The turkey problem — The evidence peaks just before the break. What conclusion does a turkey reach if it thinks statistically? This piece asks why the day with the most evidence is the day before the accident.

item.title: Nassim Taleb · Skin in the game
item.description: Nassim Taleb · Skin in the game — Read the position, not the opinion. He revived a very old filter. This piece asks why advice from someone who bears none of the consequences should be discounted automatically.

item.title: Tao Te Ching · Whatever peaks, turns
item.description: Tao Te Ching · Whatever peaks, turns — The top is where to start worrying. Usually read as comfort for bad times. It is more useful as an instrument, and it is sharpest when things are going well.

item.title: Tao Te Ching · The part you don't do
item.description: Tao Te Ching · The part you don't do — A list of moves to leave out. Usually translated as non-action and read as passivity. It is closer to a list of the moves that make things worse.

item.title: Tao Te Ching · Go to the low ground
item.description: Tao Te Ching · Go to the low ground — Not competing is a choice of location. Water has been praised for two thousand years. The text credits it with one specific thing, and it is about position.

item.title: Tao Te Ching · The empty part is the useful part
item.description: Tao Te Ching · The empty part is the useful part — What you left out is doing the work. Which part of a wheel is doing the work? The chapter is short enough to be a definition and it underwrites the whole book.

item.title: Tao Yuanming · Eighty Days as Magistrate
item.description: Tao Yuanming · Eighty Days as Magistrate — What he resigned was that day, not the office. Whether to turn now or wait for a better moment. Why Tao Yuanming left after eighty days instead of finishing the term.

item.title: Tao Yuanming · He Made a Poem of the Day He Begged
item.description: Tao Yuanming · He Made a Poem of the Day He Begged — Begging for Food. Going broke on the road you chose. How poor Tao Yuanming actually got, and what he did with that fact.

item.title: Tao Yuanming · By Mistake I Fell into the Dusty Net
item.description: Tao Yuanming · By Mistake I Fell into the Dusty Net — Know what you do not want first. You cannot say what you want. What Tao Yuanming actually knew when he knew it was time to go.

item.title: Technological Revolutions · The bubble is in the script
item.description: Technological Revolutions · The bubble is in the script — Frenzy is how installation gets funded. Canals, railways, steel, cars and the internet each ran mad in turn. This piece asks why Perez calls the madness part of the process.

item.title: Peter Thiel · Competition is for losers
item.description: Peter Thiel · Competition is for losers — Both sides lie, in opposite directions. Business school teaches you to compete. He says competing is the loss. The usable part is how to hear through what both sides say.

item.title: Peter Thiel · The important truth few agree with
item.description: Peter Thiel · The important truth few agree with — The question he asks in every interview. He opens with a question that has no model answer. What it is screening for, and what a good answer looks like.

item.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow · What you see is all there is
item.description: Thinking, Fast and Slow · What you see is all there is — Nothing announces the missing information. Kahneman gave the mind's largest defect an acronym. This page is about why ignorance produces no sensation at all.

item.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow · Losses loom larger
item.description: Thinking, Fast and Slow · Losses loom larger — Losing hurts about twice as much. The same hundred hurts about twice as much going out as coming in. This page is about what that decides for you.

item.title: Thinking in Systems · Structure drives behaviour
item.description: Thinking in Systems · Structure drives behaviour — Stop blaming the parts. The same problem has now survived three different people. This is Meadows on why that is the moment to stop blaming anyone.

item.title: Thinking in Systems · Leverage points
item.description: Thinking in Systems · Leverage points — Right place, wrong direction. She ranked twelve places to intervene in a system, weakest to strongest. This is why almost nobody uses the strong ones.

item.title: Thomas Gordon · The I-message
item.description: Thomas Gordon · The I-message — Say the effect, not the character. The same event, said one way, starts a fight; said another, starts action. Where the structural difference is.

item.title: Thomas Gordon · Whose problem is this
item.description: Thomas Gordon · Whose problem is this — Different owner, opposite method. Your child is upset, you explain, and each explanation pushes them further away. What to do in that moment.

item.title: Lev Vygotsky · The zone of proximal development
item.description: Lev Vygotsky · The zone of proximal development — Look at the second line. Two people at the same level today may end up far apart. Which measure the difference shows up in.

item.title: Lev Vygotsky · Scaffolding: give it, then take it away
item.description: Lev Vygotsky · Scaffolding: give it, then take it away — Left up, it becomes dependence. How much help is the right amount? The test is whether it comes down.

item.title: Wang Jian · Six hundred thousand or nothing
item.description: Wang Jian · Six hundred thousand or nothing — Give the real number. Asked how much you need, too much looks incompetent and too little loses. This is why Wang Jian held to a frightening number.

item.title: Wang Jian · Asking for fields and houses
item.description: Wang Jian · Asking for fields and houses — Hand them a hold over you. Holding almost every soldier in the state, how do you let the king sleep? This is about choosing to look greedy.

item.title: Wang Xing · Watch the core, not the boundary
item.description: Wang Xing · Watch the core, not the boundary — The test for expansion. With Meituan fighting on four fronts at once, everyone asked where its boundary was. What he replaced the question with.

item.title: Wang Xing · Avoiding the real thinking
item.description: Wang Xing · Avoiding the real thinking — The illusion of diligence. One line he wrote on a microblog is quoted more than anything else he has said. How busyness became a substitute for thought.

item.title: Wang Yangming · Knowing and doing are one thing
item.description: Wang Yangming · Knowing and doing are one thing — Not done means not known. 'I understand it, I just can't do it.' Wang Yangming argued that the sentence itself is the error.

item.title: Wang Yangming · You are polished by events
item.description: Wang Yangming · You are polished by events — Sitting still trains nothing. Someone said he felt perfectly steady sitting quietly and fell apart the moment anything happened. Why that steadiness doesn't count.

item.title: Wang Yangming · Act on what you already know
item.description: Wang Yangming · Act on what you already know — The answer is in your first reaction. Most of what we call being unable to decide is being unwilling to admit. Why he said the judgement is already there.

item.title: Wang Yangming · The bandits inside
item.description: Wang Yangming · The bandits inside — The hardest battle is the interior one. He never lost a campaign. Why he said all of those were the easy ones.

item.title: The Wealth of Nations · Not from benevolence
item.description: The Wealth of Nations · Not from benevolence — Aim at their interest. The most quoted sentence in economics is about dinner. Read closely, what it hands you is a protocol for asking.

item.title: The Wealth of Nations · The pin factory
item.description: The Wealth of Nations · The pin factory — What division of labour costs. The book opens in a small workshop. This is how the forty-eight thousand were counted, and what the same author says they cost.

item.title: Why Nations Fail · The two Nogaleses
item.description: Why Nations Fail · The two Nogaleses — A natural controlled experiment. A fence cuts one city in two and income differs threefold. This is what that single case rules out.

item.title: Why Nations Fail · Why elites block progress
item.description: Why Nations Fail · Why elites block progress — Not stupid, afraid. A tsar refused railways; an emperor refused factories. This is why the people blocking a technology are the ones who understand it.

item.title: Norbert Wiener · He wrote to the union first
item.description: Norbert Wiener · He wrote to the union first — Before automation landed. Is there a move to make before a technology reaches you? What the man who built it did first.

item.title: Norbert Wiener · What a machine can do, and what to give it
item.description: Norbert Wiener · What a machine can do, and what to give it — Two separate questions. Which work belongs to a tool and which doesn't. Why Wiener said capability doesn't settle it.

item.title: Norbert Wiener · Control is a loop, not an order
item.description: Norbert Wiener · Control is a loop, not an order — Seeing the result beats issuing instructions. Why the thing you carefully explained still comes back wrong. How Wiener defined control instead.

item.title: Wu Zetian · Promote out of turn, drop just as fast
item.description: Wu Zetian · Promote out of turn, drop just as fast — Fast in, and fast out. Many of the people she raised were later demoted or killed. This is about why a method that looks chaotic actually worked.

item.title: Wu Zetian · How did the chancellor lose this man
item.description: Wu Zetian · How did the chancellor lose this man — Recruiting from the pamphlet attacking you. A document tearing you to pieces is put in front of you. This is about what she said at the cruellest line in it.

item.title: Xiang Yu · Break the pots, sink the boats
item.description: Xiang Yu · Break the pots, sink the boats — Everything on one throw. Julu was the high point of his life. This is about why the thing that won it so completely never changed afterwards.

item.title: Xiang Yu · Brocade worn at night
item.description: Xiang Yu · Brocade worn at night — Deciding in order to be seen. He was urged to make Guanzhong his capital and went home instead. This is about what his reason gave away.

item.title: Xunzi · Where the rules came from
item.description: Xunzi · Where the rules came from — Scarcity wrote them, not virtue. Rules feel like morality handed down. His answer names no morality at all: only wants, shortage, and no line drawn.

item.title: Xunzi · Borrow the horse, don't grow legs
item.description: Xunzi · Borrow the horse, don't grow legs — Leverage beats effort. Two people of equal ability, and one of them gets much further. He says the difference is not in the person.

item.title: Xunzi · A group is a set of clear lines
item.description: Xunzi · A group is a set of clear lines — Headcount without division is a crowd. Slower than an ox and weaker than a tiger, people use both. The one-word answer he gives, and what follows from it.

item.title: Xunzi · Heaven runs to its own schedule
item.description: Xunzi · Heaven runs to its own schedule — Sort the fixed from the movable. Bad year, bad market, bad luck. He closed this exit two thousand years ago, and not by denying the conditions.

item.title: Zeng Guofan · Solid camp, dull fight
item.description: Zeng Guofan · Solid camp, dull fight — A clumsy method that removes the uncertainty. He fought almost no brilliant battles and finished with the army still standing. This asks why the dullest method is the hardest to break.

item.title: Zeng Guofan · Watched when nobody is watching
item.description: Zeng Guofan · Watched when nobody is watching — The stretch of the day with no observer. He set himself twelve daily disciplines and kept the record for thirty years. This asks why changing yourself is the one item available daily.

item.title: Zeng Guofan · Take in widely, employ carefully
item.description: Zeng Guofan · Take in widely, employ carefully — Judge people inside real work. A great many provincial governors came out of his staff. This asks how he judged a man before the man had anything to show.

item.title: Zhang Juzheng · The evaluation ledgers
item.description: Zhang Juzheng · The evaluation ledgers — Hang every item on a name and a date. Orders go down and nobody carries them out. This is about the ledger he used to fix a failure every dynasty had.

item.title: Zhang Juzheng · The single whip
item.description: Zhang Juzheng · The single whip — Merge the accounts into one payment. Why does the same sum shrink the more hands it passes through? This is about merging dozens of levies into one.

item.title: Zhang Liang · The old man on the bridge
item.description: Zhang Liang · The old man on the bridge — The test before the test. An old man puts a young man through a series of pointless humiliations. The question worth asking is what was being tested.

item.title: Zhang Liang · Lend me the chopsticks
item.description: Zhang Liang · Lend me the chopsticks — Take the plan apart into conditions. A proposal sounds entirely right. How do you show that it is wrong? This is the method he ran at the table, in one sitting.

item.title: Zhang Liang · Liu county is enough
item.description: Zhang Liang · Liu county is enough — Asking for the small thing at the summit. You are told to name your own reward. Do you take the largest one available? Here is why he took the smallest.

item.title: Zhang Yiming · Delayed gratification
item.description: Zhang Yiming · Delayed gratification — The trait he rates highest. Asked which quality he values, he keeps giving one answer. What the phrase actually means in his hands.

item.title: Zhang Yiming · An ordinary mind for extraordinary things
item.description: Zhang Yiming · An ordinary mind for extraordinary things — The ninth-anniversary speech. A company known for ferocity spent its ninth anniversary on composure. The specific kinds of interference he named.

item.title: Zhu Yuanzhang · Be slow to take the title
item.description: Zhu Yuanzhang · Be slow to take the title — Do without the name for now. Everyone who rose at the same time was claiming a throne. He was the one who did not, and it was worth eleven years.

item.title: Zhu Yuanzhang · Heavy punishment for officials
item.description: Zhu Yuanzhang · Heavy punishment for officials — A broken age needs a heavy hand. He put officials to death by the tens of thousands. This is about how he himself defined the range this method applied to.

item.title: Zhuangzi · The use of being useless
item.description: Zhuangzi · The use of being useless — What nobody requisitions lives longest. Making yourself useful is instinct. What being useful costs you at the same time.

item.title: Zhuangzi · The cook and the ox
item.description: Zhuangzi · The cook and the ox — Go along the gaps. One cook replaces his blade monthly, another hasn't in nineteen years. Where exactly the difference sits.

item.title: Zhuangzi · Things being equal
item.description: Zhuangzi · Things being equal — Whose ruler is this. Two people argue to the end and neither is convinced. Why Zhuangzi says a third person won't settle it either.

item.title: Zhuge Liang · The plan at Longzhong
item.description: Zhuge Liang · The plan at Longzhong — The first half is what not to touch. A twenty-seven-year-old lays out a strategy that governs the next several decades. Its hardest work is done in the opening section.

item.title: Zhuge Liang · Near the worthy, far from the small
item.description: Zhuge Liang · Near the worthy, far from the small — It is about who can reach you alone. Eight characters usually read as a moral instruction. What he means is narrower and more mechanical: who is able to see you privately.

item.title: Zhuge Liang · The tears, and then the demotion
item.description: Zhuge Liang · The tears, and then the demotion — He put himself on the same list. Executing the man he had promoted is not the hard part of this story. What he did immediately afterwards is.

item.title: The Comprehensive Mirror · Talent and character
item.description: The Comprehensive Mirror · Talent and character — The dangerous man is the able one. The first argument in the first book of the whole work is about choosing people. This is about why it sits there.

item.title: The Comprehensive Mirror · Worth copying, worth avoiding
item.description: The Comprehensive Mirror · Worth copying, worth avoiding — Fix the selection rule first. One thousand three hundred and sixty-two years of events. This is about the single rule that decided what went in.

item.title: Albert Einstein
item.description: Albert Einstein (Germany · 1879–1955) — Imagination. The physicist, and the father of relativity — but the legacy that travels furthest is not a formula, it is a way of working.

item.title: Alfred Adler
item.description: Alfred Adler (1870–1937 · Austria) — Whose task is this. The founder of individual psychology, an early colleague of Freud's who broke with him over a disagreement about direction.

item.description: Arthur Kleinman (1941– · Harvard) — Curing fails, care does not. A Harvard medical anthropologist and a practising psychiatrist, with years of fieldwork in China. His whole career splits one thing into two.

item.description: Attachment Theory (1950s–1970s · Bowlby and Ainsworth) — The early template. Bowlby worked with children who had lost their families in the war and argued that the pull towards closeness is an instinct, not a dependency to be outgrown.

item.title: Augustine
item.description: Augustine (354–430 · Hippo, North Africa) — Grant me chastity, but not yet. A bishop in Roman North Africa, and the author of the Confessions, which he wrote in his forties about the first half of his own life.

item.title: BJ Fogg
item.description: BJ Fogg (2019 · Stanford Behavior Design Lab) — Too small to fail. Founder of the Behavior Design Lab at Stanford, working on how behaviour gets designed rather than willed.

item.description: Benjamin Graham (United States · 1894–1976) — Margin of safety. The father of security analysis, author of Security Analysis and The Intelligent Investor.

item.description: C.S. Lewis (1898–1963 · Oxford) — The notebooks after she died. A writer and professor at Oxford and Cambridge, author of Narnia and of many books arguing people into belief.

item.description: Charlie Munger (Contemporary · 1924–2023) — Invert. Buffett's partner for more than half a century, and the reason Berkshire stopped buying cheap broken companies and started buying good ones at fair prices.

item.description: Chris Voss (2016 · Never Split the Difference) — Label it first. A former lead international kidnapping negotiator for the FBI, with a career spent on sieges, abductions and hostage-takings.

item.description: Elon Musk (Contemporary · 1971–) — First principles. Co-founder of PayPal, Tesla, SpaceX and Neuralink. The method is a single move repeated: go back to what is physically true and re-derive everything from there.

item.title: Epictetus
item.description: Epictetus (c. AD 55–135 · Rome and Nicopolis) — What is yours, what is not. Born a slave; his owner was Epaphroditus, a secretary to Nero. One leg was lame and stayed lame.

item.description: Excellent Sheep (2014 · William Deresiewicz) — Can clear, can't choose. A critique of elite education by someone who taught at Yale for ten years and sat on admissions.

item.description: George Soros (1930– · Budapest and New York) — Reflexivity. Founder of the Quantum Fund, and the man who forced the Bank of England to give way, making a billion dollars in a day.

item.description: Guan Zhong (Spring and Autumn · 723–645 BC) — Granaries first. The first statesman in China to think systematically about the relation between the economy and government.

item.description: Haruki Murakami (Japan · 1949–) — Writing as physical work. He ran a jazz bar into his early thirties, decided at a baseball game in 1978 that he could write a novel, and in 1981 closed the bar to write full time.
